Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

desire noun and verb

also longing, craving, eagerness, desire to do, passion

classical

Cic. Att. 12.26.1: vel studiō potius et cupiditāte nōn dubitō
Traupman 151, 152, 156

cupiditās, cupiditātis f.

noun, third declension: with the genitive of the thing or a gerund (cupiditās videndī)

desire, eagerness, longing

The general word for wanting something strongly, in a good sense (cupiditās vērī videndī, Cic. Tusc. 1.44) and, more often, a bad one: greed, ambition, lust (Lewis & Short). The verb is cupiō (see want).

Other words

  • dēsīderium, dēsīderiī n. — longing for something absent or lost

    noun, second declension: with the genitive · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 5.11.1: nōn dīcī potest quam flagrem dēsīderiō urbis; Traupman 155

    Desire for what one has had and misses: a person, home, a place (see homesickness, I miss you). Its verb is dēsīderāre, to long for, to miss.

  • cupīdō, cupīdinis f. — desire, longing

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Liv. 1.6.3: Rōmulum Remumque cupīdō cēpit … urbis condendae

    (vōx plērumque historicōrum et poētārum: Sall., Liv., Verg.)

    The historians’ word, often in the phrase cupīdō cēpit, “the desire took him”; masculine in the poets. Cicero uses it only of the god Cupid (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Rōmulum Remumque cupīdō cēpit in iīs locīs ubi expositī ubique ēducātī erant urbis condendae

    Romulus and Remus were seized by the desire to found a city in the place where they had been left and brought upLiv. 1.6.3

  • adeō quantō rērum minus, tantō minus cupiditātis erat

    the less people had, the less they wantedLiv. praef. 12

  • nōn dīcī potest quam flagrem dēsīderiō urbis

    words can’t say how I burn with longing for RomeCic. Att. 5.11.1

See also want, wish, homesickness, I miss you, look forward to, pleasure.
